title: How food changes wine
subtitle: Why the same wine tastes different with dinner
objectives: Explain why food changes how wine tastes
Name the food elements that matter most
Explain the idea of matching weight

steps.title: Food changes the wine
steps.body: Taste a wine on its own, then with food, and it often changes. A red can turn harsh after a bite of something sweet, or soft after a bite of salty cheese. Pairing isn't about finding a perfect match; it's about avoiding clashes and finding combinations where both taste better.

steps.title: The mechanism
steps.body: Your palate adapts to what it has just tasted. After sugar, the next thing tastes less sweet and more sour. After salt, it tastes less bitter and acidic. Fat coats the mouth, so tannin and acidity feel softer and cleaner. These effects are reliable enough to plan around.
steps.highlight: The palate adjusts to the last bite

steps.prompt: After eating something salty, a wine is likely to seem:
steps.explanation: Salt reduces our sense of bitterness and acidity, which is why salty dishes make many wines seem softer and fruitier.

steps.title: Weight with weight
steps.body: A simple rule that rarely fails: match the weight of the food to the body of the wine. A delicate fish needs a light white; a rich stew needs a fuller red. Big flavours overpower light wines, and big wines flatten delicate food. Colour matters far less than weight.
steps.highlight: Light with light, rich with rich

steps.prompt: Which of these food elements make a wine seem harder, more bitter or more acidic?
steps.explanation: Sweetness and umami make wine feel harsher. Salt and acidity in food make it feel softer.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Food changes how wine tastes, for better or worse
Sugar and umami harden wine; salt and acid soften it
Match the weight of the food to the body of the wine
